text: The Pylos Combat Agate (SN18-112) is an engraved amygdaloid sealstone of banded agate discovered in 2015 in the undisturbed LH II grave of the so-called Griffin Warrior near the Palace of Nestor at Pylos, together with other sealstones and four gold rings on the right side of the warrior near his right arm.

The authors consider the Pylos Combat Agate to be a Cretan work of Late Minoan I and argue that it may be the finest example of glyptic art yet discovered in a Minoan or Mycenaean context, and arguably the finest work of Aegean glyptic ever found.

The face of the Pylos Combat Agate bears a combat scene composition formed by a victorious warrior, his opponent, and a fallen warrior beneath them, with an undulating groundline and empty upper and side registers.

The engraving on the Pylos Combat Agate is on a very minute scale, with measurements such as a 1.01 cm scabbard, a 0.29 cm victor’s head, a 1.33 cm figure-of-eight shield, and a 0.045 cm diameter sealstone worn on the victor’s wrist.
At excavation, the Pylos Combat Agate was found facedown, heavily encrusted with lime, and appeared undecorated until cleaning by conservator Alexandros Zokos revealed the engraved design.

Sealstone SN18-112 is pierced horizontally and contained two oval gold caps with 14 small granulated beads each around their circumference, still in position over a thin bronze bar remaining in the string hole at the time of excavation.

The authors state that the level of detail in the Pylos Combat Agate’s representation of weapons, clothing, and human physiognomy is without parallel in known Minoan-Mycenaean art and that many details are only clearly visible using photomicroscopy and close-up camera lenses.

The victor in the Pylos Combat Agate scene strides forward from the left with legs spread, wears low boots with indicated straps, has crimped flowing locks, a double-wrapped necklace with variously shaped beads, bracelets including one bearing a lentoid seal, and a belted codpiece with backflap, with a scabbard tied to his waist by a double-looped cord with attached beads flowing behind him.

The authors argue that the Pylos Combat Agate’s combat scene draws on an iconography of battle scenes known from the Shaft-Grave period mainland and Neopalatial Crete, and that its engraving clarifies elements of dress, weaponry, and ornamentation that are unclear in other Aegean battle scenes.

The authors explicitly state that they do not claim any direct or unambiguous reading of the Pylos Combat Agate scene against the Homeric epics and suggest that different audiences may have perceived different meanings, though they believe viewers would recognize familiar heroic elements comparable to other early Late Bronze Age combat scenes.

This source is an academic article by Kazimierz Lewartowski (Studies in Ancient Art and Civilization 23, 2019) discussing the Pylos Combat Agate and a series of Late Bronze Age Aegean seal images depicting duels between warriors, their iconography, possible shared mythological background, and sociocultural significance for Mycenaean and Minoan elites. It analyzes specific seals catalogued in the Corpus der Minoischen und Mykenischen Siegel (CMS), comparing compositional schemes, fighting techniques, equipment realism, chronology, and the potential existence of a common heroic story or myth that circulated orally across regions such as Mycenae, Pylos, Vapheio, Crete, and Gouvalari. The article argues that these repeated scenes of a lightly protected swordsman defeating a better-armoured spearman served ideological functions related to violence, elite identity, leadership, and behavioral models, and may reflect episodes from a now-lost epic oral tradition comparable in function to later Homeric poetry.
“Das Corpus der minoischen und mykenischen Siegel” erfasst und publiziert Siegel und Siegelringe aus dem ägäischen Raum.
Die Sammlung wurde 1957 in Marburg gegründet und ist seit Ende 2011 an der Universität Heidelberg angesiedelt.
Das Corpus umfasst heute mehr als 12.000 Siegelabdrücke, die entweder direkt von den Originalen oder von antiken Abdrücken genommen wurden.
Zusätzlich zu den Siegelabdrücken enthält das Corpus mehrere tausend Negative, Fotografien und Zeichnungen, die das Material in außergewöhnlicher Dichte erschließen.
Das Corpus ermöglicht es Forschenden und Studierenden, die Bildwelt der ägäischen Glyptik zu vergleichen und zu analysieren, ohne auf Reisen zu internationalen Sammlungen angewiesen zu sein.
Das Corpus macht ein zentrales visuelles Medium der minoischen und mykenischen Kulturen in seiner ganzen Vielfalt zugänglich und dauerhaft erforschbar.
Der Sitz des Instituts für Klassische und Byzantinische Archäologie befindet sich am Marstallhof 4, 69117 Heidelberg.

In 1939, on the first day of excavation on a hill in western Messenia, Carl W. Blegen uncovered a Mycenaean palace that he called The Palace of Nestor.
The archives of the Palace of Nestor contained clay tablets inscribed in the so-called Linear B script, a syllabary employed to record the Greek language.
The clay tablets from the Palace of Nestor were unintentionally baked in a conflagration that destroyed the palace early in the 12th century B.C.
Carl W. Blegen planned to publish in a final volume of his excavation report all Linear B texts from Pylos, but he died in 1971 before this could be completed.

The volume "Excavations at the Palace of Nestor in Western Messenia: The Inscribed Documents" fulfills Blegen’s planned final publication of the Linear B texts from Pylos and is the work of several generations of scholars.

After a preliminary detailed introduction, Linear B tablets 1–1589 from Pylos are presented in the volume, accompanied by color photographs, transcriptions, and definitive epigraphical and palaeographical notes.
The Palace of Nestor IV is described as fundamental for any future study of Mycenaean economy and society.

text: The paper discusses the so‑called Ring of Nestor (CMS VI, no. 277) and documents arguments for its authenticity.

The Ring of Nestor has been previously associated with obscure and even legendary circumstances of discovery, which contributed to erroneous identifications of it and some other Creto‑Mycenaean gold rings as fakes.
According to the abstract, the tendency to consider the Ring of Nestor and the Ring of Minos as forgeries has been completely reassessed in favour of their authenticity.

The revision of the Ring of Nestor’s authenticity has been reinforced by recent finds of comparable iconographic subjects, such as wall‑paintings, gold rings, figurines and ivories, and by more thorough study of the techniques and craftsmanship of early Late Bronze Age signet rings.
The Ring of Nestor is described as belonging to the first centuries of the Late Bronze Age, specifically the 16th–15th century BC.

The key pictorial unit on the Ring of Nestor examined in the paper is what Arthur Evans called a “watch-dog” or “dragon”, interpreted as the guardian of an old “tree of the world” whose branches contain a populous scene in Aegean glyptic art.

The paper identifies this motif on the Ring of Nestor as a scorpion, described as a major apotropaic symbol in Bronze Age Aegean iconography, which kills the so‑called “Minoan Dragon” of the ring and supports an interpretation of the ring’s iconography.
